title: Finite-range and mean-field spin-glass Hamiltonians
notes: The lecture starts with nearest-neighbour random couplings and then passes to all-pairs Gaussian couplings scaled by \(N^{-1/2}\).
statement: The finite-range Edwards--Anderson model uses a specified lattice and neighbouring pairs. The zero-field Sherrington--Kirkpatrick model has \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^N\), independent standard Gaussian \(J_{ij}\), and \(H_N(\sigma)=N^{-1/2}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j\). Independence, centering and the summation convention determine the normalization. The thermodynamic ground energy is normalized by \(N\).
fate: The precise Gaussian mean-field setting is the one treated in \citet[Introduction]{auffingerchen2017ground} and \citet{talagrand2006parisi}. Their theorems do not automatically solve the short-range model introduced in the first line.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: The thermodynamic ground-state energy of the SK model
notes: The notes ask to study \(N\to\infty\) and \(\lim\min H\), without the extensive normalization.
statement: For the Gaussian SK Hamiltonian just specified, \(N^{-1}\max_\sigma H_N(\sigma)\) has a deterministic limit, and the minimum has the negative limit by symmetry. For covariance function \(\xi(q)=q^2/2\), the positive ground-energy constant equals \[\inf_{\gamma}\left\{\Psi_\gamma(0,0)-\frac12\int_0^1 t\xi^{\prime\prime}(t)\gamma(t)\,dt\right\},\] where \(\gamma\ge0\) is nondecreasing, right-continuous and integrable, and \(\Psi_t=-\tfrac12\xi^{\prime\prime}(\Psi_{xx}+\gamma\Psi_x^2)\), \(\Psi(1,x)=|x|\), in the appropriate weak solution sense.
fate: \citet[Theorem~1]{auffingerchen2017ground} proves the zero-temperature Parisi formula, first circulated in June 2016 and published in November 2017. It gives a variational characterization rather than an elementary closed numerical constant. The finite-temperature Parisi formula was proved earlier by \citet{talagrand2006parisi}, published in 2006.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the normalized mean-field ground-energy problem has a rigorous Parisi variational solution. The omitted factor 1/N is essential; this conclusion does not cover arbitrary finite-range spin glasses.

title: Exact finite-volume ground-state degeneracy and near-ground states
notes: The notes describe many ground states with energies differing by about \(1/N\), and assert positive limiting entropy of their set.
statement: For finite \(N\ge2\), independent continuous Gaussian couplings in the zero-field complete-graph SK model give almost surely exactly one minimizing pair \(\{\sigma,-\sigma\}\). Consequently the entropy per spin of exact minimizers is \(N^{-1}\log2\to0\). States with slightly different energies are near-ground states; their count depends on a specified energy window and normalization, which the notebook does not provide.
fate: \ours{} For \(\tau\ne\pm\sigma\), some product \(\tau_i\tau_j\) differs from \(\sigma_i\sigma_j\), so the energy difference is a nondegenerate Gaussian and vanishes with probability zero. There are finitely many pairs; spin-flip symmetry supplies the only forced equality. Independently, equality of every pair product forces \(\tau_i/\sigma_i\) to be constant in \(i\), checking the algebraic step. This elementary annotation corrects the literal sentence without replacing the much richer asymptotic-state problem treated in \citet{panchenko2013ultrametricity}.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the finite-volume claim is false under the stated Gaussian SK assumptions. The notebook\textquoteright s unspecified near-ground energy window is insufficient to define a separate quantitative entropy problem.

title: Ultrametricity of the limiting overlap array
notes: For three states, two overlaps are equal and the third is larger; the statement is attributed to Parisi and Virasoro and phrased in terms of ground states.
statement: Let a random probability measure on the unit ball of a separable Hilbert space satisfy the Ghirlanda--Guerra identities for all bounded overlap tests. For independent replicas with overlaps \(R_{ab}\), \(R_{12}\ge\min(R_{13},R_{23})\) almost surely. Permuting the replicas gives the ultrametric triple property. The hypothesis is a statement about the thermodynamic Gibbs or asymptotic overlap measure, not about every finite set of near-minimizers.
fate: \citet[Theorem~1]{panchenko2013ultrametricity}, first circulated in December 2011 and published in 2013, proves this implication without a finite-support assumption on the overlap distribution. Its introduction explains the averaging or small-perturbation mechanisms producing the identities in spin-glass models. These precise hypotheses prevent an unjustified universal finite-ground-state claim.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the ultrametricity theorem under the Ghirlanda--Guerra identities is established. The notebook\textquoteright s informal state terminology is interpreted through this rigorous limiting framework, not as an exact statement for all finite samples.

title: The spin-glass transition and the scope of the Parisi formula
notes: A final line announces a transition to a spin-glass phase without specifying temperature, field, dimension or order parameter.
statement: In mean-field SK theory the free-energy variational problem distinguishes replica-symmetric and symmetry-broken regimes. A precise transition assertion requires the covariance normalization, external field and criterion for the order parameter. The notebook line alone does not fix a numerical critical temperature or state a finite-dimensional transition theorem.
fate: \citet{talagrand2006parisi} proves the mean-field Parisi formula and makes its thermodynamic content rigorous. This identifies a substantial later development of the topic, but does not justify treating an unspecified phase-transition sentence as a solved universal claim.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, rigorous mean-field free-energy theory is established. No exact finite-range phase-transition question is assigned to this unqualified line.

title: Stochastic quantization attribution
notes: The notes credit Parisi with inventing stochastic quantization.
statement: The named construction introduces an auxiliary stochastic time and a Langevin process whose equilibrium formally reproduces the Euclidean field-theory measure. The original proposal is jointly associated with Parisi and Wu; defining a process and proving equilibrium for a singular field theory requires additional analysis.
fate: This is the established proposal of \citet{parisiwu1981perturbation}, and recurs from the matrix discussion in occurrence 1982-565.2. It is a historical remark, not an assertion that every interacting field theory has already been constructed by this method.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: The rigidity of naive quaternionic differentiability
notes: Transition maps have differentials that are morphisms of left quaternionic modules. The notes conclude that all automorphisms are linear and that simple connectedness gives a linear space.
statement: For a connected open set, sufficiently smooth maps with everywhere quaternionic-linear differential are affine in fixed quaternionic coordinates. Translations must be allowed. An affine atlas on a simply connected manifold supplies a developing map into \(\mathbb H^n\), not automatically a global identification with all of \(\mathbb H^n\); completeness is an additional global requirement.
fate: \citet[Section~3, Theorem~1]{sudbery1979quaternionic} gives the precise one-variable affine-rigidity result. \citet[Introduction and Section~1]{salamon1986quaternionic} explains why such affine structures are too restrictive for quaternionic geometry. The notebook\textquoteright s local point is right, but ``linear omits translations and the global simply-connected conclusion omits completeness.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: Quaternionic projective charts and inversion
notes: The space of quaternionic lines is labelled \(\mathbb CP^n\); the two charts on its projective line are related by \(q\mapsto q^{-1}\), with derivative \(-q^{-1}(dq)q^{-1}\).
statement: The space is \(\mathbb HP^n\). On \(\mathbb HP^1\), inversion is a transition map and its differential has multiplication on both sides. It generally fails to be a morphism of one fixed left \(\mathbb H\)-module structure. Its differential does preserve the appropriate quaternionic structure up to rotation, which motivates the enlarged structure group.
fate: \citet[Section~1, projective-coordinate construction]{salamon1986quaternionic} gives exactly this motivation and the group \(GL(n,\mathbb H)Sp(1)\). The manuscript\textquoteright s use of \(\mathbb C\) is a faithful notation error, not a translation issue.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: The ambiguous sphere obstruction
notes: The topological explanation says that \(S^3\) would have three complex structures.
statement: An almost complex structure requires even real tangent dimension, so the stated \(S^3\) cannot carry even one. The surrounding projective-line discussion suggests \(S^4=\mathbb HP^1\), but replacing 3 by 4 would be an editorial conjecture, and the intended obstruction to a global quaternionic frame would still need to be stated.
fate: The projective geometry in \citet{salamon1986quaternionic} supplies context but does not license silently changing the handwritten superscript. The recorded sentence is mathematically impossible as it stands; its intended topological proof is not identifiable.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the literal dimensional error is clear. The intended sphere and obstruction remain an unresolved reading/reconstruction issue, not an open mathematical problem.

title: Almost quaternionic structures without a distinguished triple
notes: A quaternionic subalgebra of \(\operatorname{End}(V)\) is specified, but its isomorphism with \(\mathbb H\) and the individual \(I,J,K\) are not fixed.
statement: On a real \(4n\)-manifold, an almost quaternionic structure is equivalently a rank-three subbundle \(Q\subset\operatorname{End}(TM)\) locally spanned by \(I,J,K\) satisfying \(I^2=J^2=K^2=-1\), \(IJ=K=-JI\), together with the associated rank-four algebra \(\mathbb R\operatorname{Id}\oplus Q\). Changing an oriented orthonormal local triple rotates it by \(SO(3)\). A global chosen triple is extra hypercomplex-type data.
fate: \citet[Section~1]{salamon1986quaternionic} formulates the same invariant reduction and distinguishes it from an integrable \(GL(n,\mathbb H)\)-structure. The notebook\textquoteright s explicit warning not to choose \(I,J,K\) globally is essential.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: The general and metric quaternionic structure groups
notes: The notes display both \(GL(1,\mathbb H)GL(n,\mathbb H)\) and \(Sp(1)Sp(n)\), while attaching the latter to the earlier module-linearity definition.
statement: The stabilizer of the quaternionic subalgebra is \(GL(n,\mathbb H)Sp(1)\), with the common central \(\{\pm1\}\) identified; positive scalar factors can be absorbed into \(GL(n,\mathbb H)\). After a compatible positive definite metric is chosen, the group reduces to \(Sp(n)Sp(1)\). Preserving a fixed left module structure alone gives \(GL(n,\mathbb H)\), not the compact metric group.
fate: \citet[Section~1]{salamon1986quaternionic} explicitly identifies these groups and their relation. The compact-group line in the notebook has a missing metric condition and an incorrect reference to definition (1).
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: The special role of four dimensions
notes: Every four-dimensional Riemannian manifold is said to have two quaternionic structures because \(SO(4)\) is a product.
statement: For an oriented Riemannian four-manifold, the self-dual and anti-self-dual rank-three bundles of two-forms give the two pointwise quaternionic families. The group relation is \(SO(4)\cong(Sp(1)\times Sp(1))/\{(1,1),(-1,-1)\}\). Reversing orientation exchanges the choices. A quaternionic structure in dimension four encodes an oriented conformal class, not a unique metric.
fate: \citet[Section~1 and the four-dimensional discussion]{salamon1986quaternionic} gives the exceptional relation \(Sp(1)Sp(1)=SO(4)\). The quotient and orientation data must accompany the notebook\textquoteright s shorthand ``product.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: Torsion-free quaternionic connections and twistor integrability
notes: The condition for 1-integrability is a torsion-free connection preserving the quaternionic subalgebra; parallel transport preserves it, and the connection need not be metric.
statement: For \(n>1\), a quaternionic manifold is an almost quaternionic \(4n\)-manifold admitting a torsion-free connection preserving \(Q\). This is weaker than a flat projective quaternionic atlas and does not choose a metric. Its associated sphere bundle of complex structures has an integrable twistor complex structure. In dimension four the analogous twistor integrability additionally requires the appropriate self-duality condition on the conformal curvature.
fate: \citet[Sections~2--3 and Corollary~7.4]{salamon1986quaternionic} establishes the torsion/curvature framework and the twistor construction, published before the lecture in 1986. The notebook\textquoteright s explicit ``not necessarily metric is correct and prevents a conflation with quaternionic K"ahler geometry.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: Goncharov on complexified quaternionic cones
notes: For real-analytic \(M\), Goncharov forms a cone from vectors \(v+iJv\) in a complexification and says that there must be integrability.
statement: The family of complex eigenspaces as \(J\) ranges over the quaternionic sphere is a natural twistor-type object. A precise theorem would specify whether the proposed condition is involutivity of a distribution on an incidence space, existence of complex submanifolds, or vanishing of intrinsic torsion. The notebook gives no such condition or equivalence.
fate: \citet[twistor construction, Corollary~7.4]{salamon1986quaternionic} is a close mathematical antecedent. It does not identify the exact extra assertion Goncharov intended; the item remains a partially articulated proposal rather than a newly formulated general theorem.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the cone construction is recognizable, but the intended integrability criterion is not sufficiently specified for an exact fate assignment.
speaker: A. B. Goncharov

title: Commuting partially defined isometries and unitary completion
notes: Gelfand asks how two commuting isometries in an n-dimensional space can be turned into commuting unitaries, adding explicitly that they are not defined everywhere; Kasparov is said to have done part of it.
statement: A precise extension problem must state each initial domain and range, the meaning of commutation on partially defined compositions, whether the ambient space may grow, and whether the goal is an extension or a compression dilation. In finite dimension an everywhere-defined isometry is already unitary. The handwritten domain qualification is therefore decisive.
fate: The notebook is not an exact formulation of the theorem on two commuting everywhere-defined contractions and cannot be replaced by it. Searches combining Kasparov, commuting partial isometries and unitary completion did not identify the referenced partial result with its domains. The question is preserved without inventing a missing formulation.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the exact problem and cited Kasparov contribution remain unidentified. This is a limitation of the source data, not a claim that all such extension problems are open.

title: Type-A Hecke algebras and braid-group representations
notes: The generators satisfy \((T_i+1)(T_i-q)=0\), the adjacent braid relation and distant commutativity; inverse braid generators are sent to \((T_i+1-q)/q\).
statement: For \(q\ne0\), the type-A Hecke algebra \(H_n(q)\) is generated by \(T_1,\ldots,T_{n-1}\) with these relations. They make \(T_i\) invertible, with \(T_i^{-1}=q^{-1}(T_i+1-q)\), and define a representation of the Artin braid group. The algebras form a compatible tower under the usual inclusions.
fate: \citet[Sections~3--4]{jones1987hecke} uses exactly this presentation. The theory and its link-invariant application were already circulating by the June 1985 Bourbaki lecture \citet{connes1986indice}; the later 1987 article is the detailed source, not the first appearance.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: The unnamed Leningrad type-B extension
notes: The notes say that a type-B Hecke algebra had likewise been applied in Leningrad.
statement: Type-B Hecke and braid constructions have additional generators, relations and parameters. The sentence gives neither authors nor the target links, boundary conditions or trace, so it cannot identify one exact extension of the type-A invariant.
fate: \citet[Section~5, concluding discussion]{jones1987hecke} explicitly distinguishes other Coxeter types as further directions. This thematic connection does not establish which Leningrad result the notebook refers to.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the intended local attribution remains unidentified. No new open type-B problem is assigned to this passing report.

title: Links as braid closures
notes: A link is called an immersed compact oriented one-manifold in three-space, and closing a braid gives a link.
statement: A tame oriented link is an embedded finite disjoint union of circles in oriented three-space, considered up to ambient isotopy. Closing an oriented braid gives such a link, and Alexander\textquoteright s theorem represents every oriented link by a braid closure. General immersions with double points are singular links and require different equivalence data.
fate: \citet[Section~2]{jones1987hecke} states the braid-closure setting. The manuscript\textquoteright s ``immersed must be strengthened to ``embedded for the knot invariant discussed here.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: Markov equivalence of braid representatives
notes: Conjugation inside \(B_n\) and stabilization \(b\mapsto b\sigma_n^{\pm1}\) are said to generate equivalence of closures.
statement: Two braids have ambient-isotopic oriented closures exactly when they are related by a finite sequence of conjugations, positive or negative stabilizations, and inverse destabilizations, allowing the braid index to change. Therefore a compatible trace alone handles conjugation, while stabilization needs an additional normalization.
fate: \citet[Section~2]{jones1987hecke} invokes Markov\textquoteright s theorem as the topological foundation of the trace construction. This was established before the lecture; the notebook correctly identifies the difficult converse, not just the easy invariance of individual moves.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: The algebraic Ocneanu trace has a second parameter
notes: For every \(q\), the notebook asserts a unique factor representation with trace, whose values are Laurent polynomials in \(q\).
statement: For fixed Hecke parameter \(q\), the compatible algebraic trace is characterized only after a second parameter \(z\) is supplied: \(\operatorname{tr}(1)=1\), \(\operatorname{tr}(ab)=\operatorname{tr}(ba)\), and \(\operatorname{tr}_{n+1}(aT_n)=z\operatorname{tr}_n(a)\). This is an algebraic Markov trace, not automatically a positive state or a unique von Neumann factor representation. Values on braid words also involve the inverse parameter \(q^{-1}\).
fate: \citet[Theorem~5.1]{jones1987hecke} proves precisely the trace theorem and explicitly makes \(z\) independent of \(q\). The earlier exposition \citet{connes1986indice} explains the relation to subfactors without asserting the notebook\textquoteright s universal factor uniqueness.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: From Markov traces to two-variable link polynomials
notes: The desired function of braids is invariant under both Markov moves and becomes a Laurent-polynomial knot invariant.
statement: The normalized trace expression includes factors depending on braid index and exponent sum so that both stabilization signs act trivially. The general Hecke trace gives the two-variable HOMFLY-type invariant; the Jones polynomial is a particular specialization/quotient. Equality of these invariants is a necessary condition for isotopy, not a complete classifier of links.
fate: \citet[Section~6]{jones1987hecke} gives the normalized construction and skein relation, tracing the two-variable discovery to the 1985 work of Freyd, Yetter, Hoste, Lickorish, Millett, Ocneanu and Przytycki--Traczyk. \citet{connes1986indice} shows that this was established before Kirillov\textquoteright s lecture.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: Specialization at plus and minus one
notes: The exercise asks for the invariant obtained by setting \(q=\pm1\), mentioning the ratio of Jones-polynomial values.
statement: After choosing the usual Jones variable \(t\) and normalization \(V_{\text{unknot}}(t)=1\), a knot satisfies \(V_K(1)=1\) and \(|V_K(-1)|=|\Delta_K(-1)|\), its determinant. The Hecke parameter \(q\), trace parameter and link-polynomial variable must first be related; without that choice the raw exercise does not determine one numerical specialization.
reconstruction: The Jones normalization and the distinction between its variable and the Hecke parameter are supplied editorially.
fate: \citet[Section~12, special values]{jones1987hecke} gives the specialization results. They are established identities rather than an open question. The statement here is an explicit modern normalization of the exercise, not an assertion that the notebook\textquoteright s variables were already fixed this way.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: Roots of unity and the existence of subfactor representations
notes: The notes say Jones excludes roots of unity; Gelfand suggests studying precisely them and wonders whether factors disappear there. Vershik is mentioned without a theorem.
statement: Generic semisimplicity and generic representation formulas may exclude roots of unity, but the Hecke algebra and Markov trace do not thereby disappear. Roots of unity are central to the discrete subfactor-index regime \(4\cos^2(\pi/m)\), \(m\ge3\), and yield important quotient representations. Positivity and factor realizability require specified involutions, parameters and quotients.
fate: \citet[Section~4 after Theorem~4.5 and later root-of-unity sections]{jones1987hecke} explicitly says these parameters are important and repeatedly studies them. \citet{connes1986indice} already relates the discrete indices to the braid construction. The broad exclusion attributed to Jones is false; the unnamed Vershik contribution is not uniquely identified.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, roots-of-unity representation and knot theories are established. The notebook\textquoteright s suggestion is historically interesting, but it is not an undeveloped general direction.

title: Integral Chern classes and the holomorphic Hodge filtration
notes: For a holomorphic bundle on a compact complex analytic manifold, Chern classes are integral and lie in the indicated Hodge-filtration term; cohomology is computed by the holomorphic de Rham complex.
statement: For a complex manifold \(X\) and holomorphic bundle \(E\), \(c_i(E)\in H^{2i}(X,\mathbb Z)\) has complex image in \(F^iH^{2i}(X,\mathbb C)\). Here \(F^i\) means the image of hypercohomology of the truncated holomorphic de Rham complex, not automatically an injectively embedded hypercohomology group. A Hodge direct-sum decomposition requires additional hypotheses, such as compact K\"ahler.
fate: \citet[Sections~1--2 and~8]{esnaultviehweg1987deligne} gives the Deligne-cohomology setting and the compatible Chern classes; the MPI 87-2 preprint is explicitly cited in the following lecture. The underlying integral and filtration properties are established antecedents, not new conclusions of the 1987 announced work.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: Atiyah classes, Chern characters, and invariant polynomials
notes: The transition form \(A=g_{ij}^{-1}dg_{ij}\) is treated as an ordinary matrix-valued Cech cocycle, and \(c_i(E)=\operatorname{Tr}(A^i)\) is written.
statement: The transition forms represent the Atiyah class in \(H^1(X,\Omega_X^1\otimes\operatorname{End}E)\), with the correct conjugation identifications between trivializations. After the chosen \(2\pi i\) and sign normalization, \(\operatorname{tr}(A^i)/i!\) represents the degree-i Chern character, not the Chern class. Chern classes are the elementary invariant polynomials, for example \(c_2=\tfrac12((\operatorname{tr}a)^2-\operatorname{tr}(a^2))\) for normalized \(a\).
fate: The distinction between universal Chern classes and trace-polynomial representatives is part of the characteristic-class construction in \citet[Section~8]{esnaultviehweg1987deligne}. The notebook\textquoteright s trace-power equality is false for general \(i>1\); fixing it also requires the twisted endomorphism coefficients, not only a factorial.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: An explicit cochain comparison with integral characteristic classes
notes: The problem is to construct explicitly a homotopy between the differential-form characteristic cocycle and an integral characteristic cocycle. The lecture announces Beilinson, MacPherson and Schechtman\textquoteright s Notes on motivic cohomology.
statement: The comparison asks for cochains witnessing equality of the complex image of an integral Chern cocycle and the chosen filtered de Rham representative. A Deligne Chern class packages precisely the integral cocycle, filtered representative and comparison homotopy. An explicit low-weight polylogarithmic formula is a stronger construction than the abstract existence of this lift.
fate: The announced work was published as \citet{beilinsonmacphersonschechtman1987motivic} in 1987, but its original proof text was not recovered here, so a general formula-by-formula match is not asserted. \citet[Proposition~8.2]{esnaultviehweg1987deligne} gives existence and functorial uniqueness, while \citet[Section~1.7 and Section~4]{goncharov2016exponential} provides an inspected explicit second-Chern construction. The final lecture records its weight-two ingredients.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, Deligne Chern classes and explicit low-weight comparison cocycles are established. The source-specific match to every higher-weight formula of the announced 1987 paper remains limited by access; no general unsolved problem is inferred from that limit.

title: The first Chern class from logarithms of transition functions
notes: For \(c_1\), the notes use \(d\log\det g_{ij}\) and propose dropping the exterior derivative to recover an integral discrepancy.
statement: On a sufficiently fine cover, choose holomorphic logarithms \(\ell_{ij}\) of the determinant transitions. On triple overlaps, \(\ell_{ij}+\ell_{jk}+\ell_{ki}\in2\pi i\mathbb Z\), with signs adjusted to the chosen Cech convention. Dividing that discrepancy by \(2\pi i\) gives the integral first Chern cocycle, and \(d\ell_{ij}\) its de Rham comparison. Changing logarithm branches changes the cocycle by a coboundary.
fate: \citet[weight-one complex and Chern classes]{esnaultviehweg1987deligne} identifies this construction with the exponential sequence. It is the classical complete model for the higher comparison question, and recurs in record 712.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: The lecture bibliography and its chronology
notes: The notes cite Soul\'e\textquoteright s February 1985 Bourbaki talk, Esnault--Viehweg\textquoteright s preprint, Beilinson\textquoteright s Current Problems volume 24 paper, and a tentative Contemporary Mathematics volume 25.
statement: The directly identified sources are Soul\'e\textquoteright s Bourbaki expos\'e 644, delivered in February 1985 and printed in Ast\'erisque 133--134 (1986), and Esnault--Viehweg, MPI 87-2. Beilinson\textquoteright s Notes on absolute Hodge cohomology is in Contemporary Mathematics 55, Part~I (1986), not 25. These references show that much of the Deligne-complex exposition is pre-existing material.

title: The analytic Deligne complex and its degree convention
notes: The complex is \(\mathbb Z\to\mathcal O\to\Omega^1\to\cdots\to\Omega^{p-1}\), with the first arrow multiplying by \((2\pi i)^p\).
statement: For a complex manifold \(X\) and integer \(p\ge1\), let \(\mathbb Z(p)=(2\pi i)^p\mathbb Z\subset\mathbb C\), and put \(\mathbb Z(p)_{\mathcal D}=[\mathbb Z(p)\to\mathcal O_X\to\Omega_X^1\to\cdots\to\Omega_X^{p-1}]\) in cohomological degrees \(0,\ldots,p\). Its hypercohomology is \(H^n_{\mathcal D}(X,\mathbb Z(p))\). Weight zero is the constant sheaf \(\mathbb Z\). The algebraic open-variety version requires the corresponding logarithmic construction.
fate: \citet[Section~1.1 and Section~2]{esnaultviehweg1987deligne} fixes these conventions and distinguishes analytic from algebraic Deligne--Beilinson cohomology. The notebook\textquoteright s ordinary \(H\) notation must be read as hypercohomology when the argument is a complex.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: Weight-one and weight-two cohomology sheaves
notes: The exponential map identifies the weight-one complex with \(\mathcal O^*[-1]\); for weight two the notes give \(\mathbb C/\mathbb Z(2)\) and \(\Omega^1/d\mathcal O\).
statement: The exponential sequence gives \(\mathbb Z(1)_{\mathcal D}\simeq\mathcal O_X^*[-1]\). In weight two, the cohomology sheaves are \(\mathcal H^1=\mathbb C/\mathbb Z(2)\) and \(\mathcal H^2=\Omega_X^1/d\mathcal O_X\). They are sheaves, not the global Deligne groups of \(X\); the latter require hypercohomology. Locally the holomorphic Poincar\'e lemma identifies the second quotient with the image of \(d:\Omega^1\to\Omega^2\).
fate: \citet[Section~1.1 and the weight-one comparison in Section~2]{esnaultviehweg1987deligne} verifies the exponential quasi-isomorphism. The weight-two assertions are the cohomology sheaves of the displayed three-term complex, with the notebook\textquoteright s Tate factor retained.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: Topological and curvature maps from the Deligne complex
notes: One map projects to the integer component; a second takes the exterior derivative of the final differential form.
statement: There is a forgetful morphism \(\mathbb Z(p)_{\mathcal D}\to\mathbb Z(p)\) and a curvature morphism \(\mathbb Z(p)_{\mathcal D}\to\Omega_{X,\mathrm{cl}}^p[-p]\), zero except on the last component, where it is \(d\). Calling the first target \(\mathbb Z\) is harmless only after identifying the Tate lattice with the abstract integers; comparison in complex cohomology must retain \((2\pi i)^p\).
fate: \citet[Sections~1--3]{esnaultviehweg1987deligne} constructs the corresponding projections and compatible products. These are pre-existing structural maps, and the last-component derivative automatically takes values in closed forms.

title: A chain-level Deligne product and commutativity up to homotopy
notes: The notes give ordinary multiplication when either factor is an integer, then \(x\wedge dy\) when the right form has top degree, and claim commutativity up to homotopy.
statement: For positive weights \(p,q\), one standard asymmetric product of the truncated complexes is \(x\cup y=xy\) when \(\deg x=0\); it is \(x\wedge dy\) when \(\deg x>0\) and \(\deg y=q\); it is zero otherwise. In particular a positive-degree left factor multiplied by a degree-zero right factor is zero in this model. This product is a chain map; its opposite is chain-homotopic to it, inducing graded commutativity on hypercohomology.
fate: \citet[Section~1.1 and Section~3, especially Proposition~3.5 and Theorem~3.9]{esnaultviehweg1987deligne} gives product conventions and their homotopies. The notebook combines the asymmetric top-form rule with two-sided integer multiplication and thereby violates the chain-map convention; one cannot keep all three literal rules simultaneously.

title: Functorial Deligne Chern classes and the meaning of uniqueness
notes: Holomorphic bundles have classes \(c_p(E)\in H^{2p}_{\mathcal D}(X,\mathbb Z(p))\), determined by functoriality and their ordinary Chern-class images.
statement: There is a universal natural system of Deligne Chern classes compatible with pullback, the topological Chern classes and the usual characteristic-class identities. The uniqueness is a universal functorial statement. On a fixed \(X\), specifying a topological image alone does not select a unique Deligne class because the kernel can be a nonzero intermediate Jacobian.
fate: \citet[Proposition~8.2 and its proof using the universal bundle]{esnaultviehweg1987deligne} proves the stated existence and uniqueness. The preprint was available as MPI 87-2 and is explicitly named at the lecture\textquoteright s start, so this is E rather than a new 1987 conjecture.

title: Cech hypercohomology and the signed total differential
notes: The double complex is totalized using \(d+\delta\), with component relations linking an integral cocycle and forms on multiple overlaps.
statement: For Cech degree \(r\), a standard total differential is \(D=\delta+(-1)^r d\), unless one has already signed one of the two component differentials. On an acyclic cover or a suitable resolution, total cohomology computes the hypercohomology of the Deligne complex. The component equations must include the same signs and the initial Tate-lattice inclusion.
fate: \citet[Sections~1--2]{esnaultviehweg1987deligne} uses the complex-of-sheaves framework. The notebook\textquoteright s abbreviated unsigned formula is acceptable only with an unstated anticommuting convention; with the ordinary commuting Cech and de Rham differentials it is incorrect.

title: The Deligne exact sequence and the intermediate Jacobian
notes: For compact \(X\), Hodge decomposition is asserted and Deligne cohomology is an extension of integral Hodge classes by a quotient called the Griffiths Jacobian.
statement: For compact K\"ahler \(X\) and \(p\ge1\), there is an exact sequence \[0\to\frac{H^{2p-1}(X,\mathbb C)}{F^pH^{2p-1}(X,\mathbb C)+\operatorname{im}H^{2p-1}(X,\mathbb Z(p))}\to H^{2p}_{\mathcal D}(X,\mathbb Z(p))\to\{c\in H^{2p}(X,\mathbb Z(p)):c_{\mathbb C}\in F^p\}\to0.\] The left group is the intermediate Jacobian. The right description retains torsion; a literal intersection inside complex cohomology would lose it.
fate: \citet[Section~7 and the basic exact sequences]{esnaultviehweg1987deligne} gives the Jacobian interpretation. Compactness alone does not guarantee the Hodge decomposition used in the notebook, and all complex comparisons need the Tate lattice.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: A Deligne cocycle as an explicit comparison homotopy
notes: The notes describe an integral cocycle, a filtered de Rham cocycle and a homotopy between them, then write a differential of a sum beginning with \(\alpha_0\), although the preceding homotopy sum begins with \(\alpha_1\).
statement: The intermediate components form a total cochain of degree one less than the compared cocycles. With consistent total-complex signs, its differential is their difference. The degree-n integral cocycle \(\alpha_0\) is one endpoint and cannot be included as an ordinary degree-\(n-1\) homotopy term. This is the mapping-cone interpretation of Deligne cohomology, not an equality between unsorted forms of different total degrees.
fate: \citet[cone construction in Section~2]{esnaultviehweg1987deligne} provides the precise framework. The notebook\textquoteright s reference to Gabrielov--Gelfand--Losik points to earlier combinatorial characteristic-class comparisons; it is an antecedent, not an identification of every Deligne homotopy with one of their formulas.

title: Picard group and the Deligne first Chern class
notes: The determinant bundle controls \(c_1\); logarithms of transition functions give the cocycle, but the final formula reads \(\log(\deg g_{ij})\).
statement: For a complex manifold, \(H^2_{\mathcal D}(X,\mathbb Z(1))\cong H^1(X,\mathcal O_X^*)=\operatorname{Pic}(X)\). Under this identification a line bundle gives its Deligne first Chern class; for a higher-rank bundle it is the class of \(\det E\). The logarithm is \(\log\det g_{ij}\), and its Cech discrepancy lies in \(2\pi i\mathbb Z\).
fate: \citet[weight-one exponential comparison and Section~8]{esnaultviehweg1987deligne} gives the result. The manuscript\textquoteright s \(\deg\) is a faithful slip; it is not a meaningful degree of a variable transition matrix in this formula.

title: Motivic complexes and the regulator refinement
notes: Chern classes should first take values in \(\mathbb Z(p)_M\) and then map through a polylogarithmic regulator to Deligne cohomology. Weight zero is \(\mathbb Z\), weight one is \(\mathcal O^*[-1]\), and negative effective weights are set to zero.
statement: For smooth algebraic varieties over a field, motivic cohomology and its complexes now have rigorous constructions, including cycle and transfer models. In weight one, \(\mathbb Z(1)\simeq\mathbb G_m[-1]\); motivic Chern classes admit realization/regulator maps to the corresponding complex-analytic cohomology. The convention of zero negative weights belongs to the effective complex formulation, not to the assertion that negative Tate objects vanish in a stable motivic category.
reconstruction: The switch from arbitrary analytic manifolds to smooth algebraic varieties, the topology of the motivic sheaves and the effective/stable distinction are necessary modern specifications.
fate: \citet[Lectures~3--4,~15 and~19]{mazzavoevodskyweibel2006motivic} develops the established theory from Voevodsky\textquoteright s 1999--2000 lectures, published in 2006. The explicit low-weight regulator is inspected in \citet[Proposition~1.7]{goncharov2016exponential}. Existence of this theory does not prove every vanishing property proposed in the next notebook line.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise statement above is established; the qualifications distinguish it from the abbreviated notebook formulation.

title: Beilinson--Soule vanishing in nonpositive degrees
notes: For positive weight \(p\), the proposed motivic complex has cohomology only in degrees \([1,p]\).
statement: The unresolved lower-degree assertion includes the Beilinson--Soul\'e vanishing conjecture: for every field \(F\), \(p>0\), and \(j\le0\), \(H^j(F,\mathbb Q(p))=0\). The notebook\textquoteright s integral sheaf-amplitude formulation is stronger in its coefficient and sheaf details. Upper-degree bounds and the existence of motivic complexes must be separated from this nonpositive-degree vanishing.
fate: \citet[Section~4 and Theorem~4.1]{garkusha2023semilocal} states the amplitude conjecture and proves equivalent criteria, not the general conjecture (2020 preprint, 2022 online publication, 2023 journal issue). \citet{soule2026interview} explicitly describes the conjecture as still open in an interview dated 4 November 2026. Known arithmetic cases do not establish it for all fields.
present_status: Open in general as of 12 November 2026, with direct near-cutoff confirmation from Soul\'e. The construction of motivic cohomology itself is established and must not be reported as solving this vanishing conjecture.
worth: Worth preserving with its exact coefficient and degree scope: it is a definite surviving part of the notebook program, but no bounded proof of the general vanishing assertion is attempted.

title: Milnor K-theory and the top motivic cohomology sheaf
notes: The notes generate the Milnor algebra by units with the Steinberg relation \(\{a,1-a\}=0\), mention additivity in a product, and identify the top weight-p sheaf with Milnor K-theory.
statement: For a field \(F\), \(K_*^M(F)\) is the tensor algebra over \(\mathbb Z\) on the abelian group \(F^*\), modulo the two-sided ideal generated by \(a\otimes(1-a)\), \(a\ne0,1\). Symbols are multiplicatively additive in each entry and the resulting algebra is graded-commutative. For smooth varieties the appropriate unramified sheaf is used; the field comparison is \(H^p(F,\mathbb Z(p))\cong K_p^M(F)\). Graded commutativity does not mean that every odd square vanishes integrally.
fate: \citet[Lecture~5, Theorem~5.1]{mazzavoevodskyweibel2006motivic} proves the field comparison and fixes the Milnor symbols. The tensor presentation already includes additivity in units; a free algebra on the underlying set of units without those relations would be the wrong object.

title: The weight-two Bloch complex and the five-term relation
notes: The degree-one group is generated by functions avoiding \(0,1,\infty\), modulo the alternating cross-ratio relation from five points; the differential is \(t\mapsto t\wedge(1-t)\).
statement: Over a field, let the pre-Bloch group be generated by \([z]\), \(z\ne0,1\), modulo the five-term cross-ratio relations. The map \([z]\mapsto z\wedge(1-z)\) kills those relations and defines a two-term weight-two complex. The opposite sign convention \((1-z)\wedge z\) is equally valid if used consistently. Integral comparisons require careful antisymmetric-tensor and 2-torsion conventions; the exterior-square model is safest after inverting 2 or rationalizing.
fate: \citet[Section~1.5]{goncharov2016exponential} constructs the sheafified Bloch complex and its regulator. \citet[Introduction and Theorem~5.2]{suslin1991bloch} explains the exact integral K-theory relation and its torsion terms. The notebook itself already warns about 2-torsion, which should not be dropped.

title: Suslin and the indecomposable K3 group
notes: Suslin is credited with connecting the Bloch complex to K-theory, and the construction is called Bloch--Suslin.
statement: For an infinite field \(F\), the Bloch group obtained as the kernel of the weight-two symbol boundary is closely related to \(K_3^{\mathrm{ind}}(F)=\operatorname{coker}(K_3^M(F)\to K_3(F))\). After tensoring with \(\mathbb Q\), Suslin\textquoteright s comparison identifies these groups. Integrally there is a roots-of-unity torsion term and a convention-sensitive modification; one must not identify the whole pre-Bloch group or all of \(K_3(F)\) with the kernel.
reconstruction: The rational comparison is stated without the convention-sensitive integral extension. The classification records prior circulation, rather than inferring a post-1987 discovery from the printed date.
fate: \citet[Introduction, p.~217, and Theorem~5.2, p.~237]{suslin1991bloch} is the precise later publication: Russian original 1990, English issue 1991 (translation copyright 1992). Suslin explicitly says that most results of the paper were obtained in 1982. The April 1987 notebook independently witnesses the prepublication circulation of the Bloch--K-theory connection. It is therefore treated as exposition of an already circulating result, while the introduction does not date every refinement of the final theorem separately. The theorem was read directly and specifies an infinite field, the indecomposable quotient and the modified roots-of-unity torsion term.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the precise field comparison is established. The notebook omits the distinction among pre-Bloch, Bloch and indecomposable K-theory groups, which the statement restores.

title: The dilogarithmic regulator map
notes: The final diagram maps the weight-two motivic complex to the Deligne complex using logarithms and the dilogarithm.
statement: A chain-level regulator must include logarithmic correction terms and branch data so that the differential of the dilogarithmic term agrees with the symbol boundary and the five-term relation is respected in the target complex. A single uncorrected branch of \(\operatorname{Li}_2(z)\) is not a globally single-valued map to the Deligne complex. The real Bloch--Wigner version gives a single-valued real regulator after the appropriate real realization.
fate: \citet[Proposition~1.7 and its preceding formulas]{goncharov2016exponential} supplies an explicit weight-two morphism of complexes. The classical five-term and single-valued real formulas are treated in \citet{zagier2007dilogarithm}. Earlier seminar occurrences 1974-342 and 1979-477 concern dilogarithms/regulators but are not the same full motivic-complex conjecture.

title: A cross-ratio cocycle for the second Chern class of a rank-two bundle
notes: For a rank-two bundle and local sections \(s_i\), the notes place one component on triple overlaps in units wedged with units and another on quadruple overlaps in the Bloch group, obtained from four projective points.
statement: Choose local nonzero sections in sufficiently general position so that all required pairwise determinants and cross-ratios are defined and invertible on the refined intersections. A triple of sections supplies an exterior product of determinant functions; a quadruple supplies a Bloch symbol of their cross-ratio. The Pl\"ucker identity identifies the symbol boundary with the Cech boundary of the triple component, and the five-term relation supplies the next cocycle identity. Degenerate configurations require refinement or the appropriate resolution, not evaluation at forbidden cross-ratios.
reconstruction: The general-position, nonvanishing and refinement conditions are supplied from the explicit cocycle construction.
fate: \citet[Section~1.7, equations~(1.34)--(1.44), and Section~4]{goncharov2016exponential} provides an inspected explicit construction matching the notebook\textquoteright s last sketch, including the regulator to Deligne cohomology. The lecture announces the earlier \citet{beilinsonmacphersonschechtman1987motivic}; its exact original formula was not inspected, so the later source is not presented as first discovery.
present_status: As of 12 November 2026, the rank-two weight-two construction is explicit and established. This is a completion of the recorded sketch, not a claim that a polylogarithmic formula in every weight follows from it.
